title: Approximating VC and Littlestone dimensions
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Historical Question 1: can either VC dimension or Littlestone dimension of an explicitly listed finite Boolean concept class be approximated within some fixed constant factor in polynomial time? Under randomized ETH, the answer is negative for each dimension, already by Theorem 2 of the cited paper. “Either” allows choosing one dimension once; it does not require one algorithm to estimate both simultaneously.

source_formulation.text: Nonetheless, it remains open whether any constant factor approximation is achievable in polynomial time:
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

context:
Question 1 appears in the introduction to motivate the paper. Theorem 2 rules out constant-factor approximation under randomized ETH, and other theorems establish stronger guarantees under stronger or alternative hypotheses.

For a nonempty class with \(m\) distinct concepts, both dimensions are at most \(\lfloor\log_{2}m\rfloor\). Zero-dimensional cases can be recognized directly, and outputting one on the remaining cases gives an \(O(\log L)\)-factor estimate. Thus a coarse logarithmic approximation does not supply an arbitrary fixed constant factor.

Theorem 2 excludes polynomial-time approximation within \(o(\log L/(\log\log L)^{\xi})\) for some constant \(\xi>0\), under randomized ETH. Under the paper’s randomized Gap-ETH or Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis, Theorems 3 and 4 strengthen this to \(o(\log L)\). Those extra hypotheses are not needed for the constant-factor negative answer.

The conclusion notes that computing a near-optimal mistake-bound number is not known to be equivalent to constructing an efficient online learner with a near-optimal mistake bound. This unresolved approximate-strategy question is not substituted for the extracted numerical approximation task.
why: Shows a computational obstruction to evaluating basic combinatorial measures of learning difficulty, even when the entire class is explicitly available. Constant-factor hardness matters because these measures are often used only up to such factors when assessing statistical or online learning requirements.

definitions:
The input lists a finite domain \(X\) and a nonempty finite class \(\mathcal C\) of Boolean functions on \(X\), by its full binary incidence matrix \(M_{x,c}=c(x)\). The target is not given by a succinct circuit or by a sampling oracle. Domain size and number of listed concepts both vary with the input; duplicate concept columns may be removed. Let \(L\) denote the total explicit encoding length, with \(L\geq2\) for asymptotic notation.

The VC dimension is the largest integer \(d\geq0\) for which some set \(S\subseteq X\) of size \(d\) is shattered: every function \(S\to\{0,1\}\) occurs as the restriction of a concept in \(\mathcal C\).

For Littlestone dimension, consider a deterministic online learner with no computational restriction. On each round it receives \(x_{t}\in X\), predicts a bit, then learns the true bit \(y_{t}\). The finite sequence is realizable when a single concept \(c\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(c(x_{t})=y_{t}\) on every round. The learner's mistake bound is the maximum number of wrong predictions over all realizable sequences of any finite length. Littlestone dimension is the minimum such bound over all learners.

Equivalently, Littlestone dimension is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree whose internal nodes are labeled by elements of \(X\), whose outgoing edges have labels \(0,1\), and for which every root-to-leaf sequence of examples and edge labels is realized by some concept. The concept may differ between paths. These are combinatorial definitions of the number being estimated; constructing an approximately optimal online learner is a separate algorithmic problem.

Fix one of the two dimensions and write its value as \(D\). A constant-factor approximation means that there is a fixed \(r\geq1\), independent of the matrix dimensions and input, and a uniform polynomial-time algorithm outputting a binary-encoded rational \(\widehat D\) with
\[D/r\leq\widehat D\leq D.\]
For a randomized algorithm, this must hold with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. Time is polynomial in \(L\) in the worst case. No shattered set or online strategy must accompany the numerical estimate. When \(D=0\), successful approximation requires output zero.

Randomized ETH, the assumption used here, asserts that no randomized \(2^{o(N)}\)-time algorithm decides satisfiability of all \(N\)-variable 3CNF formulas with bounded error. Polynomial dependence on the explicit formula length is allowed; repetitions can be removed so that its size is polynomial in \(N\). The paper's Section 2.2 expressly treats reductions and the associated hypothesis as randomized. A deterministic-only version of ETH is not silently substituted.

The conditional negative result rules out every fixed factor \(r\), including large constants, for each of the dimensions separately. It is not an unconditional lower bound, and it is not merely hardness of finding the exact integer value.
answer_criterion: The source already proves the negative answer under randomized ETH. A positive constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm for either dimension would contradict that assumption. The historical question is therefore recorded as conditionally resolved rather than as an unreviewed open challenge; no unconditional nonexistence assertion is made.
